      "evidence": "Traced path. (1) internal/steward/runner.go TickSeconds returns 600 when no config is set; the real checkout has no metasystem.steward.tick-seconds override. (2) In the base commit, both the helm path and the normal path ended in runnerWait(top, interval, ...). That loop sleeps 200 ms per step until start+interval and returns early only on a stop request or a provider-limit change, so the old runner already idled between ticks. (3) The commit's TestRunnerPassCost (runner_idle_test.go:420-437) logged, on this machine: '211 open alerts, 267 proof payloads (1 MiB each): health alert read=20.9ms census supplement=271ms'. (4) The real stores the cache covers hold 0 to 33 small files (alerts 248 KB in total, mains 68 KB), not 1 MiB records. (5) The new wait (runner.go, wait closure) sleeps interval-work, which is never longer than the old sleep. Result: neither change can account for, or remove, a continuous 54 to 63 percent load. The per-tick timing line is useful instrumentation, but the brief's 'name the pass that burns' and the item's outcome ('a steward runner must idle between ticks') are not delivered. The burn is likely in per-cycle work outside the two bounded passes (bridge Step, TrimCaches, DeliverPending, the channel phase, or a background goroutine), and none of that was measured.",

      "title": "The unit does not show that it fixes item AU, and its own measurement points away from the passes it changed. The brief says to measure first and name the pass that burns, because the steward runners were using 54 to 63 percent of a core continuously. The commit bounds the alert (health) and worker-census reads and changes the sleep. But its measurement shows those passes take about 5 to 21 ms (health) and about 270 ms (census) per tick, and the census figure is only that high because the fixture makes every record 1 MiB. At the default 10-minute tick, that is under 0.1 percent of a core. The loop before this commit already slept the full interval after every tick.
